items.stem: Risk tolerance and risk capacity differ in that risk capacity refers to:

options.text: The client's financial ability to withstand losses
options.rationale: Correct: capacity is the objective ability to absorb losses.

options.text: How the client emotionally feels about risk
options.rationale: That is risk tolerance, not capacity.

options.text: The current level of the stock market
options.rationale: That is a market condition, not the client's capacity.
The adviser's preference is irrelevant to the client's capacity.

items.explanation: Correct: capacity is the objective ability to absorb losses.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which two reflect good wealth-management practice? (Select TWO)

options.text: Planning around the client's goals and whole situation
options.rationale: Correct: holistic, goal-based planning is sound practice.

options.text: Keeping costs and fees under control
options.rationale: Correct: controlling costs protects long-term wealth.

options.text: Selling whichever product pays the adviser most
options.rationale: That is a conflict of interest, not good practice.
A complete plan addresses protection and estate matters.

items.explanation: Correct: holistic, goal-based planning is sound practice.

items.stem: During a sharp market downturn, the most constructive thing a wealth manager usually does is:

options.text: Coach the client to stick to the agreed long-term plan
options.rationale: Correct: steadying behaviour avoids locking in losses.

options.text: Encourage the client to sell everything immediately
options.rationale: Panic-selling often crystallises losses at the worst time.

options.text: Promise the market will recover by a fixed date
options.rationale: No one can guarantee timing of a recovery.

options.text: Stop all communication with the client
options.rationale: Communication is most important during stress.

items.explanation: Correct: steadying behaviour avoids locking in losses.
